authoredFrom: PS25 / PS26 / PS27 — pass-2 adversarial review of `exports`, `overrides` and the class-member symbol. Authored 2026-10-03 from a re-probe, before observing post-fix output. Each of the three was found by writing the strongest argument against an emitted label and measuring it (validation/m14/fixtures/powershell/adversarial-probes.ts, probes P3, P1, P2 and P11), and each row below states its CORPUS DELTA, because all three are pinned by fixture and only one of them is reachable from the corpus. PS25: `addExport`'s guard was `name.startsWith("*")`, which is POSITIONAL — over all 1,108 admitted files through production `parseFile`, `exports` edges with a wildcard in ANY position = 7 (every one the target `Measure*`) and edges whose target is exactly `*` = 0, so the refusal existed, did not fire, and `*` is not a legal character in a PowerShell function name, so `Measure*` resolves against nothing by construction. PS26: `classMembers` held bare NAMES, so `overrides` was a pure name comparison that discarded the `isStatic` and `isHidden` the analyzer had already parsed off the same node and matched across member KINDS. PowerShell's `hidden` attribute means a member is NOT inherited by derived classes, a `static` member is not virtually dispatched, and a method does not override a property. Corpus measurement: 0 `hidden` class members, 0 `static` class members, 0 same-name pairs whose kinds differ — MEASURED DELTA 0 edges. PS27: the pinned local-rebuild wasm mis-lexes a class member with NO leading modifier whose name begins `Static` or `Hidden`. `[int] StaticOpen() { return 40 }` parses as `attribute "[int]"` · `class_attribute "Static"` · `simple_name "Open"`, so the method was published as `Open` and the split `class_attribute` was read as a modifier, stamping `isStatic: true` on a method with no modifier. Root cause: grammars/tree-sitter-powershell/grammar.js:1266 builds `class_attribute` from `reservedWord`, and `caseInsensitive` (line 1839) emits `[sS][tT][aA][tT][iI][cC]` with NO word boundary, so the token matches the first six characters of an identifier. This fixture pins the analyzer's mitigation of the NAMING half; the DESTRUCTION half (`[int] Hidden2()`, `[int] Static()` leave an ERROR that swallows the next class declaration) cannot be repaired by an analyzer and is reported as a grammar finding.

expectSymbols.name: StaticOpen
expectSymbols.comment: PS27, THE ROW: pre-PS27 this symbol was named `Open` — the suffix the wasm's lexer split off. The fixture also declares `static [int] StaticOpen()` in the SAME class, which parses correctly, so the two collapse into one symbol by owner+name+kind: the assertion is that the name is `StaticOpen`, not `Open`. Pre-PS27 the `Open` assertion below is what the analyzer satisfied.

expectSymbols.name: HiddenThing
expectSymbols.comment: PS27: the `Hidden` half of the same lexer bug. `HiddenThing` splits into `class_attribute "Hidden"` + `simple_name "Thing"`, so pre-PS27 this symbol was named `Thing` and the `hidden` attribute was recorded on a method the author never hid.

expectSymbols.name: Stat
expectSymbols.comment: PS27 CONTROL: a name that merely STARTS with the same four letters and is not a modifier keyword. If the mitigation joined on a prefix test rather than on the tree's own `class_attribute` node, this would become `StaticStat`.

expectRelationships.comment: PS26 CONTROL: an ordinary same-named method IS an override — PowerShell class methods are virtual by default and there is no `override` keyword, so the standing name-match rule is unchanged. Without this row every forbid below would also pass against an analyzer that emitted no `overrides` at all, which is the vacuous pass this suite refuses.
PS26 CONTROL: the second ordinary pair on the same class pair, so a rule emitting at most one `overrides` per class pair cannot satisfy this fixture.
PS26 CONTROL: method over method across a DIFFERENT base, so the kind guard cannot be explained by refusing every non-first base.
PS26 CONTROL: no modifiers and no kind change anywhere on the pair. With this row absent, every positive above could be explained by the modifier logic rather than by the name match.

PS27 CONTROL: the inheritance edge over the very class pair whose method names the wasm splits. Narrowing `overrides` must not narrow `extends`, and the base NAME here is read off the class header, which the same lexer does not touch.
PS26 CONTROL: `extends` and `overrides` are separate types on one class pair; this row and the `Shared` override above are the pair that makes the difference visible.
PS25 CONTROL: an ordinary `-Function NAME` publishes. The four wildcard forbids below would all pass against an analyzer that published no exports at all.
PS25 CONTROL: the `-Variable` flag is a different reader branch from `-Function`, and it is the one the rows above do not reach.

forbidSymbols.name: Open
forbidSymbols.comment: PS27, THE PRE-FIX SHAPE: the method `[int] StaticOpen()` was published as `Open` because the wasm's lexer split the name. Nothing in the file declares a method called `Open` on this class, so the symbol named a method that does not exist and the real one was never declared.

forbidSymbols.name: Thing
forbidSymbols.comment: PS27: the same defect on the `Hidden` keyword — `[int] HiddenThing()` was published as `Thing`.

forbidSymbols.name: StaticStat
forbidSymbols.comment: PS27 CONTROL, negated: the mitigation joins a `class_attribute` that the TREE produced, it does not test the name text. A prefix test would manufacture this symbol out of the `Stat` method.

forbidRelationships.comment: PS26, the language's own word: `hidden` on a base member means the member is NOT inherited by derived classes, so a same-named method in the derived class is not an override of it. Pre-PS26 this published, because `classMembers` stored the name and dropped `isHidden` — which the analyzer had already parsed onto the symbol one line away. MEASURED CORPUS DELTA 0: the admitted corpus carries 0 `hidden` class members, which is why this row exists.

PS26: the BASE member is `static`, and a static member is not virtually dispatched — neither a derived instance method nor a derived static method of that name overrides it. MEASURED CORPUS DELTA 0: 0 `static` class members in the admitted corpus.

PS26, the KIND asymmetry, first direction: `classMembers` was filled from `class_property_definition` as well as `class_method_definition`, so a base PROPERTY was matchable and this derived PROPERTY published as an override. Pre-fix the asymmetry ran one way only — the base side accepted properties, the candidate side took methods (real-powershell-analyzer.ts:1424 against :1446) — so a derived method over a base property DID publish while a derived property over a base property never could. The fix removes the wrong direction and does not add the other, because a same-named derived property's observable behaviour is a judgement and the corpus carries 0 examples; the direction it does not add is asserted by the `Slot` forbid below.

PS26, the direction deliberately NOT added: a derived PROPERTY over a base property of the same name. This row states the decision rather than the accident — it passes today and would keep passing, and pinning it is what stops a later reader from 'fixing' the asymmetry by making properties candidates and publishing edges for a construct nothing in the corpus exercises.

PS26 + PS27 together: `SplitDerived.StaticOpen` exists only because the wasm split the name and the mitigation rejoined it, and `SplitBase.StaticOpen` is `static`, so the pair is refused on the BASE side. This row is the one place both fixes are load-bearing at once — without PS27 the member is named `Open` and does not collide at all, so the row would pass for the wrong reason, and the `StaticOpen` symbol row above is what rules that out.

PS25, THE MEASURED DEFECT: `Export-ModuleMember -Function Measure*` is the same kind of declaration as `-Function *` — the module publishes every function MATCHING a pattern and the expansion happens at run time. The pre-fix guard was `startsWith("*")`, so the bare `*` was refused and `Measure*` was published as a symbol name. 7 of the lane's 113 `exports` edges on the admitted corpus were this row, all of them target `Measure*`, and `*` is not legal in a PowerShell function name, so the target resolves against nothing by construction. filterNoiseRelationships does not drop a `*` target (it bans `<>{}` backtick and whitespace, not `*`), so these reached the store.

PS25: the SECOND wildcard character. The pre-fix guard tested only `*`, and a fix that handled `*` but not `?` would pass the `Measure*` row and leave the other PowerShell wildcard in place. Measured corpus count for a `?` target: 0 — the row is precautionary and says so.

PS25: the bare `*`, which the pre-fix guard DID refuse. Pinned anyway — the guard was rewritten from a prefix test to a whole-string wildcard scan, and a rewrite that dropped the case the old one handled would pass this fixture's other rows while regressing here.

forbidExports.comment: PS25: the same defect on the `exports[]` array, which pool-worker passes to the store separately from the relationship channel. Fixing only the edge would leave the array holding the pattern.

PS25: the bare `*` on the array channel.

expectRelationshipCount.comment: PS26 + PS27: exactly four, and the count is the assertion. Five `overrides` forbids would each pass against an analyzer that emitted none, and four positives would each pass against one that emitted every pair — only a count pins the rule to `same name AND same kind AND base is neither hidden nor static`. Pre-PS26/PS27 this same file yields SIX: the two extras are `Secret` (hidden base) and `OnlyProp` (method/property kind mismatch). PS27 alone accounts for a different wrong edge — `SplitDerived -> SplitBase` on the split name — which the count also excludes.

PS25: exactly two. Five function-shaped declarations are written and three of them are wildcards, so a count is the only assertion that separates 'published the two names' from 'published everything' and from 'published nothing'.
